title: The Carpenter's Village: Mio and the Road to Steveston
standfirst: In 1888 a carpenter named Kuno Gihei left this fishing village for an undeveloped settlement on Canada's Fraser River. He himself found little but hardship there. The neighbors who followed him into salmon fishing did not: within decades Mio's houses, its school and even its nickname, America Village, bore the marks of Steveston's money. This dossier follows both shores.

sections.heading: A fishing village with little land

paragraphs.text: Mio sits on the Kii Peninsula, on a stretch of the Hidaka District coast where mountains leave little flat ground and most of the district's harbors open southwest into the Kii Channel. A 1923 geography of the prefecture describes nearby Hii and Yura as deep, sheltered bays, if cramped, and the cape further southwest, Hinomisaki, as a place that gave passing ships' passengers trouble in rough water, marked by that time with a white, rotating lighthouse beam. An Edo-period survey of the same coast describes the villages of the old Mio estate, of which Mio itself was the namesake settlement, as living chiefly by fishing or by carrying cargo in all directions, with no want of a livelihood, in contrast to an inland neighboring estate whose people worked the land instead.

The wider district's own 1923 geography sums up Hidaka in a few lines: a place known for its farm produce, its timber and its paper, with cotton-spinning concentrated around the district town of Gobo, and otherwise given over to hills and to the sea. Mio itself, a modest fishing settlement, appears in the district's own 1910 statistical yearbook as one of thirteen towns and villages counted separately, alongside Gobo, Matsubara, Wada, Hiizaki and the rest, each with its own population return; the scanned page's exact figures for Mio are no longer legible, but its listing there confirms the village's place, however small, in the district's official bookkeeping a generation before its name became better known abroad than at home.

sections.heading: The carpenter who went to look for work

paragraphs.text: The district's own 1923 history sets down what happened next, and who came first. Three other Hidaka villagers had already gone abroad: a man from Yura to the United States and one from Yoshiwara to Hawaii, both in 1885, and one from a hamlet of Hiizaki to British Canada in 1887. Behind them, 'a bit later,' came Kuno Gihei of Mio, a carpenter by trade. He had heard that the Vancouver area of British Canada was promising for fishing, farming and manufacturing; he obtained a travel permit from Kanagawa Prefecture in September 1887 and sailed the following March. He meant to work in industry, but the place he reached, the gazetteer says, was still an undeveloped small settlement, nothing like what he had expected, and he spent more than twenty hard years there.

Kuno himself never made much of a success of it. He returned to Japan in December 1911 and died of illness in August 1916, at 63. Yet the same source is direct about his significance: whatever his own fortunes, it says, Mio villagers' later development in North America owed itself largely to him as its spark. The following year, 1889, several more men left, not as general laborers but specifically to fish: Tsuchiyama Torakichi, Mizuyabu Wakamatsu, Kuroyama Yonekichi, Yamamoto Fukumatsu, Yoshida Kamekichi, Osawa Yaichi, Ueda Itaro and others. The waters were rich, the district history notes, but their boats and gear were not equal to it at first; they adapted, did well, and the reports that reached Mio each year drew more of its people after them.

Mio's pattern was not quite typical of its own district, which is part of what makes it distinct. The same 1923 history records other Hidaka villages sending their own early travelers to very different places over the same years: groups from two nearby farming villages to the United States from 1892 to work the land, one man from Nishi-Uchihara to Australia in 1893, another from Nanbu who had already failed at two businesses in Wakayama City and become a Christian minister in Hiroshima before he finally obtained a travel permit there and left for America too. Almost every case the gazetteer records begins the same way, one villager's report of success or failure reaching home and either drawing others after him or warning them off; Mio's story is simply the case, among a dozen such stories from this one stretch of coast, where the following was largest and the destination, Canada's Pacific coast fishery, most consistently the same.

sections.heading: Steveston, and the war that scattered it

paragraphs.text: The place Kuno Gihei and his neighbors were making for is known today as Steveston, a fishing settlement at the mouth of the Fraser River, now part of Richmond, British Columbia. The Canadian side's own account of the connection puts more than 2,000 people of Mio origin living in Canada by 1940, and states that Steveston once held the largest Japanese population anywhere in the country. Fishing bred its own trades alongside it: one Steveston boatworks built by the Kishi family in the 1930s turned out 24- and 26-foot wooden gillnetters, sometimes four at a time, and kept building and repairing boats there into the late 1960s; its last wooden gillnetter, the Silver Ann, was launched in 1969, long after most of the yard's original Japanese Canadian founders had gone.

The pace of the work bred its own speech, too. Fishermen coordinating a salmon run, with no time to be diplomatic, developed what has since been called the Steveston, or Kishu, dialect, a working shorthand remembered today in terms like 'ajiro' for a good fishing spot and 'gaina' as an exclamation of surprise, understood on the Fraser River by people whose grandparents had never left Wakayama.

None of this went unopposed by other British Columbians. Through the 1900s to 1920s, provincial and federal fisheries policy, often argued in the name of conserving salmon stocks, steadily reduced the number of commercial licenses granted to Japanese Canadian fishers and placed legal restrictions on their boats and gear; not until a 1928 Supreme Court of Canada ruling, holding that the province could not favor some British subjects over others in issuing licenses, did the courts push back against the practice. Steveston's Japanese Canadian community, in which Mio families were so heavily represented, absorbed this pressure for two full decades before the war made it far worse.

The Pacific war broke the pattern for good. From 1942 the Canadian government removed everyone of Japanese descent from a zone within a hundred miles of the British Columbia coast, roughly 22,000 people in all, more than half of them Canadian-born; homes, cars and fishing boats were left behind and later sold by the government without their owners' consent. Only in 1949, four years after Japan's surrender, were Japanese Canadians permitted back onto the coast and given the same rights, including the vote, as other citizens.

Mio itself changed with the money that came back. By 1909 emigrants in America had contributed more than 10,000 yen, a considerable sum, toward building the village's elementary school at Naka-no-hama, remembered in the district's own history as a memorial to their success abroad. Houses built in a recognizably North American style went up too, among them the one that stands today as the Canada Museum; there were enough of them that Mio had, by the 1920s, already earned in print the nickname a later reference work still uses: America Village, a fishing settlement, it notes, that sent out an unusual number of overseas emigrants and kept, as a result, its own distinct customs.

Kuno Gihei's own return to Japan in 1911 was not an isolated case. The house that is now the Canada Museum, a hipped-roof building with painted siding and rooms that mix Japanese and Western styles, was built in the 1930s by the Nakatsu family, who had themselves worked in Vancouver and come home; the local newspaper that covered its registration as a cultural property describes it as exemplifying a wider pattern in which returning emigrants reshaped the village's own architecture, and with it its character.

The clearest place to see this history today is the Canada Museum, in a two-story wooden house with a hipped, green-tiled roof and white-painted siding, built around 1934 by the Nakatsu family, who had themselves worked in Vancouver, and later passed to the Noda family. Mihama Town took the building over in 2017, opened it as a museum in July 2018, and had it registered as a national tangible cultural property in 2019. Its adjoining Canada Garden holds a totem pole made in Canada and, since 2022, a bronze statue of Kuno Gihei himself, donated by his own great-grandson on a visit from Vancouver. Alongside them, and not really about Canada at all, sits an old Fresnel lens from the second generation of the Hinomisaki lighthouse down the coast, a reminder that the garden gathers up the village's whole seafaring past, not only its Pacific-crossing half.

A short walk away stands Mio's former elementary school, closed as a school but still in use: a local organization now trains village children to explain the area's history in English, a direct echo of the traffic that once ran the other way, from this coast to the Fraser River. One room of the Canada Museum itself works the same way in miniature, kept as a small café where a visitor can sit with coffee among furnishings meant to recall a returnee's bygone life in Canada. The 1923 district history's account of Kuno Gihei's own hard years, set beside the neighbors who did better than he did, is worth remembering on that walk: the museum and the statue mark a success that was, for its first mover, no success at all.

sections.heading: A village measured against its own past

paragraphs.text: Mihama Town, of which Mio is now a part, counted 8,667 people at its founding in 1954; a compiled reference work puts its population at 6,867 in 2020, a decline of roughly a fifth over two-thirds of a century, in line with the slow shrinking of small fishing towns across rural Japan. Mio's own experience of that decline has run alongside a second, smaller current in the other direction: a magazine survey of the village's revival efforts reports that agreements to rent or buy empty houses in the area were roughly three times more common in 2020 than three years before, crediting the pull of the Canada Museum, its guesthouse and diving-and-marine-sports business, and the storyteller program, alongside the plain appeal of a small coastal life. Whether that current will do more than slow the larger one is not yet a question this dossier's sources can answer; what they can confirm is that the village's identity, well over a century after Kuno Gihei sailed, is still built as much around Steveston as around the Kii coast it sits on.

timeline.what: A domain survey of the coast describes Mio-estate villages living chiefly by fishing and coastal shipping.
The first Hidaka District emigration pioneers leave, for the US mainland and for Hawaii.
Kuno Gihei of Mio, a carpenter, obtains a travel permit and sails for the Vancouver area of British Canada.
Several more Mio men follow Kuno, specifically to fish; word of their success draws more each year.
A lighthouse is established at Hinomisaki, the cape near Mio.
Mio emigrants in America fund construction of the village's elementary school, over 10,000 yen.
Kuno Gihei dies in Japan at 63, five years after returning from Canada.
More than 2,000 people of Mio origin are living in Canada, many in the Steveston fishing settlement.
Japanese Canadians are removed from the British Columbia coast; only in 1949 are they permitted to return with full citizenship rights.
Mio, Wada and Matsubara villages merge to form Mihama Town.
A Mio family returned from Vancouver builds the house that later becomes the Canada Museum.
Mihama Town opens the Canada Museum in the restored house (2018) and has it registered as a national tangible cultural property (2019).
Kuno Gihei's great-grandson donates a bronze statue of him to the museum's Canada Garden.

caveats: Kuno Gihei's birth year is not stated directly in the source used here; only his death (August 1916, at age 63) is given, so no birth year is asserted in this dossier.

The Edo-period survey cited for the area's fishing economy describes the medieval 'Mio estate' and several of its constituent hamlets by name; it does not name Mio-ura itself in the specific passage read, so the connection to the village is presented here as reasonably inferred rather than explicitly stated by that source.

The Hinomisaki lighthouse's establishment is dated 1895 by Kotobank (citing Britannica); the Fresnel lens in the Canada Garden is described by its display as coming from the lighthouse's second generation.

Automated summaries of Mio-related web pages twice produced conflicting or garbled personal names for individuals connected to specific historic buildings; where a name could not be independently confirmed, this dossier omits it rather than risk a wrong romanization.

The official Mihama Town website (town.mihama.wakayama.jp) could not be reached this session; municipal-history facts instead rely on a compiled reference source (Kotobank/Britannica) that names its own underlying references.
